Khadary-whitefish Coregonus chadary begins life as a yolk-sac larva emerging from an embryonated egg with an egg diameter of 1.5 millimeters, a dimension that directly determines the initial mass of the newly hatched individual. The wet weight at birth is approximately 0.0018 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0018 grams], a value that aligns with the modest caloric reserves contained within the relatively small demersal egg characteristic of this species. This initial mass places Coregonus chadary among the smaller-bodied coregonine larvae at the moment of chorion rupture and subsequent larval eclosion, reflecting a reproductive strategy that prioritizes high fecundity over per-offspring investment. Field observations of newly emerged sac-fry indicate that the yolk-dependent period is brief, as the exotrophic transition to first exogenous feeding occurs rapidly after the completion of yolk absorption. The size of the fertilised ovum thus imposes a significant constraint on the energetic autonomy of the prolarva, which must quickly develop the capacity for prey detection and capture to avoid the point of no return. This early life-history bottleneck has been documented in several congeneric whitefishes and underscores the importance of the birth mass in determining subsequent survival probabilities.

Female Coregonus chadary undergo a prolonged period of somatic growth before reaching the size threshold that triggers the onset of gonadal activity and reproductive maturation. The total length at puberty for females is recorded at 40 centimeters [Lp = 40 centimeters], a value derived from length-at-age data collected during the transition to sexual maturity. Attaining this length typically requires several growing seasons, during which the fish allocate resources toward the accumulation of lipid stores and the development of ovarian tissue. The onset of vitellogenesis and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis coincide with the achievement of this body size, which appears to be a more reliable predictor of reproductive readiness than chronological age across the species range. Comparative studies among coregonines indicate that the length at puberty for females of Khadary-whitefish falls within the intermediate range for the genus, reflecting a life-history strategy that balances the advantages of early reproduction against the survival costs associated with smaller body size. The wet weight at puberty is 810 grams [Wwp = 810 grams], a mass that is functionally linked to the total length through established length-weight relationships specific to this species.

The maximum recorded total length of Coregonus chadary reaches 60 centimeters [Li = 60 centimeters], representing the asymptotic body size that individuals approach after many years of growth. This ultimate total length is accompanied by a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 2988 grams [Wwi = 2988 grams], a value predicted from species-specific length-weight regressions fitted to large sample collections from the Amur River basin. Attaining such dimensions requires sustained access to productive feeding grounds and the ability to avoid predation during the years required to approach this size plateau. The asymptotic mass of nearly three kilograms places Khadary-whitefish among the medium-bodied members of its genus, with larger congeners such as Coregonus nasus exceeding 6 kilograms while smaller species like Coregonus albula rarely surpass 1 kilogram. The length-weight relationship underlying these values is allometric rather than isometric, meaning that as the fish grows in length, its mass increases at a proportionally greater rate due to changes in body depth and condition. This allometric shift during the juvenile and sub-adult stages reflects the progressive accumulation of muscle mass and visceral fat reserves that support the energetic demands of reproduction.

Females produce approximately 33 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 33 eggs per day] when expressing the daily deposition rate averaged across the spawning season, which for this species extends over several weeks. This daily fecundity is a function of both the clutch size per spawning event and the frequency with which females release eggs, though in this case the rate is given as a direct daily output observed under the temperature regime of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. The wet weight at puberty and the ultimate wet weight both serve as important scaling factors that influence the total reproductive output a female can achieve over her lifetime, as larger individuals typically carry more developing oocytes. When maintained at 13 °C [T = 13 °C] throughout the reproductive period, the observed egg deposition rates are substantially higher than those recorded at cooler temperatures, indicating a strong thermal dependency of ovarian function and spawning periodicity. The spawning season spans several weeks, and the daily rate of approximately 33 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 33 eggs per day] results in a substantial total seasonal output, reflecting the species' high fecundity.

The lifespan of Coregonus chadary has been documented from long-term mark-recapture studies conducted in the Amur River and its tributaries, with the oldest individuals reaching a maximum longevity of 14 years [am = 14 years] when living under the natural thermal regime that averages approximately 13 °C [T = 13 °C] in the principal feeding habitats. This life span is comparable to other medium-sized coregonines that inhabit similar temperate river systems, though it is considerably shorter than the maximum ages exceeding 25 years reported for Arctic-dwelling populations of Coregonus clupeaformis. The age-related mortality rate increases noticeably after the onset of reproductive senescence, with senescent adult death typically occurring during the post-spawning period when physiological condition is at its annual nadir. The total length of 40 centimeters [Lp = 40 centimeters] at puberty for females represents the size at which approximately half the females in a cohort become reproductively active, and this milestone is reached several years before the ultimate total length of 60 centimeters [Li = 60 centimeters] is attained. The interplay between growth rate, age at maturity, and maximum life span defines the fundamental life-history strategy of Khadary-whitefish, which relies on iterative spawning events spread across a reproductive window of roughly a decade to maintain population stability.
